case_studies.title: LOCAA: An Agentic System for Automated Lossy Compressor Tuning
case_studies.abstract: Large-scale scientific simulations generate substantial data volumes, making lossy compression essential for reducing storage and data movement costs. However, users configure compressors through numerical error bounds (EBs) while often evaluating results using quality metrics and end-to-end performance. Because the relationship between an EB and these outcomes varies across datasets and compressors, identifying a suitable configuration typically requires exhaustive search, which can be time-consuming and computationally demanding. We present LOCAA, an Large language model-based scientific los
case_studies.summary: LOCAA tackles the tedious task of tuning lossy compression settings for large scientific datasets by using a large‑language model to predict the best error‑bound that balances storage savings and data quality. It builds an automated system that recommends compressor configurations, cutting the need for manual trial‑and‑error. The result is faster deployment of efficient compression with fewer resources spent on exhaustive search.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage storage or data pipelines that use lossy compression, integrate LOCAA into your workflow: 1. Feed your dataset metadata and desired quality metrics into LOCAA; 2. Use the generated error‑bound recommendation to configure your compressor; 3. Monitor compression ratio and output quality, adjusting only if the results deviate from expectations.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper introduces an agentic system that uses a large language model to automate the tuning of lossy compressors for large scientific datasets. While the idea is innovative and could attract curiosity among IT professionals, its direct applicability to everyday infrastructure tasks is limited. The system could eventually help reduce storage and data movement costs in cloud environments, but the current description is more proof‑of‑concept than a ready‑to‑deploy solution. Hence the novelty score is moderate, the IT relevance is somewhat high due to potential cloud cost savings, and the actionable value within 90 days is low.

case_studies.title: RunningTab: Direct Workspace Interaction with Environment-Side Tabs
case_studies.abstract: Much knowledge work produces new deliverables from files a workspace already holds, and LLM agents are beginning to take such work over. Through direct corpus interaction, an agent can search and read any of those files from a terminal with no indexing, and producing a deliverable from many of them in this way is what we call direct workspace interaction (DWI). Reaching the files, however, is only half the task: nothing keeps track of what the task asks for, what has been read, and what was listed but never opened, all of which slip through the context window without leaving a trace, so an age
case_studies.summary: The paper introduces Direct Workspace Interaction (DWI), a method that lets LLM agents read and use files in a workspace without needing to index them, and shows how it can produce deliverables directly from those files. It builds a system that tracks what the agent has accessed and what it still needs, keeping this state outside the usual context window. The result is a more efficient workflow for LLM-powered knowledge work, but the technique is focused on file‑centric tasks rather than cloud infrastructure management.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper introduces a practical method for LLM agents to interact directly with a workspace without prior indexing, which is a notable idea for infrastructure automation. It provides a concrete approach that could be integrated into existing SaaS tooling or MLOps pipelines, giving IT engineers a new way to automate file handling and task tracking. The concepts are actionable within 90 days, as they can be prototyped using current LLM APIs and integrated into Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace environments. The total score is well above the 40‑point threshold, so "low_signal" is set to false.
